title: Piston Slap: Getting Familiar with MLS Gaskets

body_markdown:
*Ryan* writes:


Earlier this year, I was rummaging through a junkyard in search of a good OEM radio and found one in a 1996 Ford Windstar, and it then occurred to me that 1996 was 30 years ago! The newest car I have is now 22 years old! At some point I missed the memo on MLS (Multi-Layer Steel) gaskets. What makes them different, and why did they become so common?


My 2004 Chrysler Sebring was running great one day, and the next it couldn’t cool off. There’s no sludge in sight. I changed the thermostat, water pump, and radiator, but none of that worked. It seemed like there might be a blockage inside the block or heads preventing coolant from circulating, so I removed the heads, and a local automotive machine shop found them to be warped .002″, and I was told, “That’s all it takes with MLS gaskets.”


Ryan the OP


Ryan the OP


Do you have a recommendation for a source of information on torque specs and tightening sequence for rebuilding an engine? Do people still use printed manuals, or is everything online?


*Sajeev* answers:


Information sources are pretty easy in my experience: Either you purchase a printed manual from a place like eBay (where book or parts resellers go to unload their inventory) or you[download a PDF](https://www.manualslib.com/manual/1588140/Chrysler-Sebring-2004.html) of the same manual. I haven’t tried it yet, but I assume you can download the PDF, send it to a local printing shop (like FedEx or a local business offering the same service) and have a bound, paper copy of said PDF made to use while you work on your vehicle. If I’ve got this wrong, I’d love to be corrected in the comments.


I wasn’t aware that Multi-Layer Steel (MLS) head gaskets could fail as they did in your Chrysler Sebring. Apparently, I too missed the aforementioned memo. MLS gaskets are designed to excel in modern engines that run hotter, have higher compression (compared to the 3.8-liter Essex V-6 in your Ford Windstar), and run forced induction. They are made of layers of steel, have a stamped-in, spring-like tension around places like the cylinder bores, and have synthetic elastomers (i.e. something rubber-like) to seal the oil and coolant passages and fill in minor differences in gap between the cylinder head and the engine block.


Everything is complicated these days, so why not engineer some of that goodness into a head gasket? In theory, these MLS gaskets have the springy flexibility to manage change in an engine over time. Your Sebring begs to differ, but we’ve been tinkering with multi-compound head gaskets for decades (as we transitioned away from asbestos in the 1980s), and hot rodders used to have a thing for head gaskets like the Fel-Pro Loc Wires. The metal wire inside them resisted blowouts for supercharged applications, but some folks preferred regular head gaskets for an important reason: They are a failsafe against serious engine damage caused by an errant mistake in a vehicle’s air-fuel ratio.


And the lesson learned by some Loc Wire head gasket users probably holds true for MLS head gaskets. It seemingly does its job well, until it decides to sacrifice itself for the well-being of your pistons. Considering how horrible head gaskets were immediately after the transition away from asbestos (which I feel, as a[fellow Essex 3.8-liter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/on-the-verge-of-unobtainum-a-mad-junkyard-dash-to-save-endangered-parts/) owner), I think the MLS design does its job pretty well. (But to my surprise, asbestos wasn’t completely banned[until recently](https://www.epa.gov/asbestos/asbestos-was-banned-do-i-need-be-worried-about-products-market-today-containing-asbestos) .)


But that brings up another issue, centering around torque-to-yield (TTY) head bolts. If you ever pull the cylinder head on a modern car, you will need new head bolts, because so many applications use TTY bolts that deform when torqued down, implying they are single-use only.


If I googled correctly, your Sebring also has TTY bolts. Not replacing them will likely shorten the lifespan of your new MLS gaskets by a significant margin. And with that, I look forward to reading everyone’s thoughts on MLS gaskets in the comments below!
